rules: Everything here is an AI draft (provisional_ai_draft): each counted item passed two blind AI checks that were tested on planted errors, and no person has reviewed it.
A finding counts only in the setting its own quoted lines show; read `setting` before carrying it to another setting.
A question's status is a label from fixed rules over its counted findings; `status_check` says whether that label itself passed its check.
Cite the paper and page from the passage, and read the PDF page before relying on a claim.
notes: No result in this paper reports uncertainty for its scores (only Table 8's examination statistics carry +/- values), so no card reaches EMPIRICAL_MULTI_SETTING. RES-FAILURE-CONSISTENT-FALSE's quote starts mid-sentence and does not name the pattern it counts ('Wrong intermediate answers', p8 L101-p9 L5); those lines and the 96-examination sample (p8 L73-77) are added as passages. Reading the garbled Table 5 lines by order (the mapping agrees with the harmonic means of P and R), the ablation's quoted drops 78 -> 68.3 (NQ) and 77.2 -> 71.1 (TriviaQA) compare the LM vs LM (Majority) row with the '- Follow-up' row; against the single-run LM vs LM row (68.5 and 72.1) the drop is about 0.2 and 1 F1 points, and the 6%-10% recall decrease also holds only against the Majority row. The paper does not say whether the ablation row is single-run or majority. Likewise the RES-VS-BASELINES examples (85.4 F1 on PopQA, 77.2 on TriviaQA) are LM vs LM (Majority) values, and the RES-FALSEHOODS ranges (87%-98%, 75%-99%) appear to match the Majority rows of Table 7 rather than single runs. In the RES-CHATGPT quote two LM vs LM F1 values are not the harmonic mean of the P and R beside them (LAMA 85.1/70.7/76.7, NQ 74.5/74.9/77.7), possibly typos in the paper. The Falsehoods dataset size is not stated in the lines read. No record seems mislabelled.

method.description: An examiner LM questions the examinee LM about the examinee's own claim in a prompted multi-turn interaction (setup questions, follow-up questions, then a 'correct' or 'incorrect' decision), and its rejections are scored with precision, recall and F1 for detecting incorrect claims, in three examiner/examinee model settings on four closed-book QA datasets.

Examiner Evaluation We evaluate how well the
examiner detects claims that are factually incorrect,
using the following metrics:4
• Precision: the portion of incorrect claims, out of
the claims rejected by the examiner.
• Recall: the portion of incorrect claims rejected
by the examiner, out of all the incorrect claims.
• F1: the harmonic mean of precision and recall.

method.description: GPT-3 and ChatGPT were prompted to give wrong answers to questions from the four QA datasets, answers containing the gold answer or an alias were discarded, and the examiner's accuracy on these false claims, which it should always reject, is reported (Table 7).

passages.text:
In addition, we created a dataset of false claims
to further test our approach. This “Falsehoods”
dataset contains only wrong claims, created separately for each model (GPT-3 and C HAT GPT)
and for each of the four QA datasets. Concretely,
given a model and a question Q, we prompt the
model to generate a false answer (see §B for details). We verify that these are indeed incorrect
claims by checking that the gold answer (and any
of its aliases, if they exist) does not occur in the
generated text. This yields a subset of examples
that are realistic, namely, the answer matches the
target type (e.g., “a city”) but is incorrect (see examples in Table 3). The examiner’s decision for
these examples should always be to reject.

To generate a wrong claim, given a query Q for one
of the QA datasets we use, we prompt our models the following way: in case Q is in a question
format, we use “Please answer the following
question with a wrong answer: <Q>” and
further request the LM to “Please also phrase
your answer as an argument.”. in case Q is
in a sentence-completion format, we use “Please
complete the following sentence with a
wrong answer: <Q>” and further concatenate Q
with the model answer. Table 12 introduces a few
